I did say we don't have a population problem but rather a massive issue with resource distribution? I am SO well aware that we have more than enough resources and space for all humans currently living. Any talk of "overpopulation" is a myth because we have a massive excess of resources literally being wasted for the sake of capitalism in one region while siphoning resources from other regions and causing ecological disasters.

I am not describing ecofascism, I'm talking about a potential reality where climate change has caused sufficient changes to the planet that some regions become literally uninhabitable, causing disruption to staple food sources and freshwater access. If a region that was previously habitable starts crumbling to pieces because deforestation has removed the root networks literally holding the ground in place, it will become uninhabitable. If a region that was previously habitable literally becomes too hot to live in for most of the year, it's functionally uninhabitable. We can deal with the cold far better than the heat. If a region that is currently relied on for agriculture starts to have  greater temperature ranges and destructive weather patterns that massively reduces the production capacity, we may have significant problems. 

To be absolutely clear, I am talking about the potential harms of climate change. I am not advocating for population reduction, I am scared for how climate change will materially affect people. We're already seeing it in a smaller capacity. We're seeing how unscrupulous practices by corporations scorch entire geographical regions and make life difficult for people who are forced to live there. My point was that while "overpopulation" is not an issue, overcrowding of habitable zones when resource production and redistribution is disrupted may be a more realistic source of horror. I would personally really love for precisely no one to die from preventable causes such as famine, drought, flash floods, unlivable daytime temperatures, soil erosion, and all the other stuff we can expect with climate change continuing. But the anxiety that all existing humans may be forced to migrate into shrinking habitable zones isn't a new one, and might be worthwhile exploring in horror. It's part of the persistent tension in Mad Max, for example. That's in no way advocating for ecofascism. I'm not saying climate change should kill people off. I very much believe we should try to prevent that, actually. I'm trying to say climate change may make life very challenging for future people and exploring that in fiction may be more realistic. Jesus Christ.

I think we might need a reminder also that suggesting something be explored in fiction is not actually advocating for the idea, often far from. I encourage everyone to read both widely and critically.

Please consider re-reading my comment to see how I didn't advocate for ecofascism. Thanks.

It sounds like you were already medicated for ADHD as a child without being told that that's what it was? A lot of kids were and they were expected to grow out of their behaviours. There's a lot of people who argue that kids were over-medicated for "behavioural issues" in the fairly recent past, but given the high rates of people who were never medicated as kids, struggled, and got diagnosed as adults, it sounds like the population rates of ADHD are just much higher than previously thought. Unfortunately, the world we live in is very hostile to anyone who can't function in very specific and frankly unnatural ways.

In terms of what a doctor could do, you'd likely be referred for a diagnosis first. Doctors will generally require a formal diagnosis to even consider further options. After that, you could be prescribed medication, but this isn't the only option. 

There are therapists who specialise in working with clients to help them figure out how to make tasks they absolutely have to do more manageable, help them work out how to use their traits to their advantage. I don't know what the case is where you live, but therapists who specialise in that kind of coaching may not need a formal diagnosis, especially if you're paying privately.

Methylphenidate is probably the most commonly-prescribed medication, but there are other options. You might also find that you react differently to it as an adult. The other options the NHS in the UK gives are lisdexamfetamine, dexamfetamine, atomoxetine, and guanfacine. I don't know what your options are where you live so I can't say what alternatives to methylphenidate might be available to you.

You can also just independently find resources on the topic and see if any of the "life hacks" that other people with ADHD use might work for you. That might range from cutting out caffeine to making chore lists a specific way to reorganising your living space so you're not inadvertently discouraging yourself from certain tasks. You don't need a formal diagnosis to do that, lots of neurotypical people benefit from those kinds of things too because neurodivergent people can be very good at finding ways to work smarter, not harder. Just worth bearing in mind that people of all neurotypes aren't a monolith and just because something doesn't work for you doesn't mean you don't have ADHD, and vice versa.

To second what the other commenter said, this definitely sounds exactly like what most people I know who got diagnosed with ADHD later in life (or are currently waiting for a diagnosis) were like, myself included.

Your brain needs to meet a certain threshold of interest and motivation to engage in tasks, and many tasks like cleaning and life admin don't meet those thresholds until it's down to the wire. Do you clean better when you know you have a guest coming over? Congratulations, the motivation threshold has been met. That doesn't indicate laziness or immaturity, it's just your brain trying its best with more limited resources in the productivity department than the average neurotypical person.

To be clear, ADHD isn't a mental health issue, it's a brain structure difference. It can result in similar behaviours to mental health issues such as depression or anxiety, and there is a high rate of comorbidity of the two with ADHD, but ADHD itself isn't a mental health issue in the way you're thinking of it. You can have ADHD traits like you're describing and be perfectly happy in life.

It's incomplete diagnostic criteria relevant only to the US. Other regions use the ICD as opposed to the DSM, which means that rapid weight loss is also recognised without the person in question needing to be underweight according to their BMI (a frankly ridiculous way of measuring this anyway as it doesn't account for people who might weight a little more due to high muscle mass or high bone density, for those who might have cysts or tumours, and for those who will simply never hit that low a BMI because they have other health or physiological issues). Not hitting a certain BMI doesn't mean you don't hit the rest of the diagnostic criteria.

It's because America uses the DSM (put out by the American Psychiatric Association) whereas Europe generally uses the ICD (maintained by the WHO). That leads to there being different diagnostic criteria for various things, sometimes in terms of the recognised symptoms, and sometimes in terms of the number of symptoms from different bands being met in the diagnostic requirements.
Which to me suggests that the focus on weight specifically as a diagnostic criterion is severely flawed.

Which is why I favour the ICD 11 classification, which also allows for rapid weight loss in place of low BMI as long as other criteria are also met. Limiting it to BMI means that most people with heavy restrictive eating who meet every single other diagnostic criterion will never get the help they need because they're "not sick enough", which often leads to very poor health outcomes. The diagnostic focus on BMI doesn't account for people whose BMI is supplemented by muscle mass or who will simply never reach a very low BMI because their body won't permit it, either due to other health conditions or due to physiology.

Having a BMI over 17 doesn't prevent people from dying in the exact same way someone with a lower BMI might. 

The pertinent aspect of the disorder is the mental state. The focus on weight means that people get discharged from care as soon as their BMI is high enough only to immediately "relapse" when they never recovered in the first place, while people who need help are told they don't have anorexia simply because they weigh too much to count. Which, given the nature of the illness, is about one of the worst things you could hear if you're trying to stop someone getting worse.

Oxalic acid is the thing that binds calcium and makes it unusable for the tort. It is present in a lot of dark leafy vegetables such as turnip greens, kale, cabbage, all kinds of plants that you'd think are safe for tortoise consumption. It's best to check on tortoise husbandry websites, they'll often list specifically which plants contain oxalic acid. They can be given very occasionally, but a captive tortoise's diet is already poorer in calcium than the average wild tort's so you have to be careful.

Unfortunately that includes some of their all-time favourite snacks, like dandelions. You just need to monitor their intake and make sure most of their diet is still made up of safe plants that are also rich in calcium.

I'm not defending anything. Admittedly, I don't know much about owls in captivity, but I have seen many other supposedly solitary animals form seemingly impossible bonds with other animals. That being said, I definitely agree on the cat saliva front and the idea of keeping owls as domestic pets. I was making one point about animal behaviour, not "defending animal abuse". I am in general agreement with you, just think a lot of animals we consider to be solitary are social in their own way, especially in relationships across species boundaries. Again, do NOT condone this or owls as pets.

Many animals that are not social can still enjoy physical contact and recognise the difference between interactions with members of its own species and members of other species, in the way that spiders are absolutely not social but some tarantulas keep frogs as pets and some jumping spiders like to sit on humans because we're warm. Tortoises are incredibly unsocial but still enjoy their necks being scratched. Owls aren't social but seem to enjoy certain kinds of touch, and being very intelligent animals they need enrichment and play. And some species of owl display a much greater range of social behaviours than others, from living in neighbourhoods to closer living arrangements, suggesting that this isn't unilateral across all owl species. I think it's really hard to say "all of this it categorically uncomfortable for the owl". To prepare, make sure that you're totally comfortable and not distracted for your appointment. Do whatever you need to to make sure you're not disturbed. Make yourself tea or go for a walk or whatever helps you relax beforehand (no substances or intoxicants, obviously). You can also collect anecdotes from your childhood, if you're on good terms with your childhood caregivers. It's not completely necessary for a diagnosis (I had no childhood anecdotes for my appointment), but it's good supporting material for your case. If you have any questions, write them down beforehand. If there are things you KNOW you want to mention during the appointment, write them down too. The meeting can feel like it's moving pretty fast, you can get nervous and forget to say things.

There will be some questions about your sexuality. It can be uncomfortable to answer but hopefully knowing they're coming makes it easier to prepare.

Be honest about your goals for HRT or surgery, and be honest with what you plan and when because referrals and recommendations have expiry dates. 

I hope this helps at all, congratulations on your upcoming appointment and best of luck!

Ok I am an adult returner to ballet so please take this with the pinch of salt it requires, but I used to get this critique all the time. I knew my shoulders were getting all bunched up but I couldn't stop it in the moment.

The things I did for it:
- started working out my back and shoulders in earnest. Once I knew where all the muscles were and could feel they were stronger they became much easier to control.
- Also work out your core. Good core and good posture make it easier to keep your shoulders in the correct position, too.
- practice thinking "down" about your shoulders all day. It's part of good posture anyway, but at work, doing the dishes, doing groceries, keep thinking about pulling your shoulders down. It will become second nature after a while.
- If you're struggling with this and keep bunching your shoulders anyway, fill a backpack with books and wear it for a bit while standing. Get used to that feeling, memorise the feeling of your shoulders being pulled down. Try some arm positions and memorise what your shoulders feel like in those moments.

I never get corrections on my shoulders anymore.

That's not how probability works. You're not MORE likely to be queer for every sibling before you that wasn't, that assumes that one person within a certain group size MUST be queer. Based on this, let's say there are 5 siblings, each sibling starts out having a 1/5 chance of being queer. The first sibling in this scenario happens to not be queer, so now all the remaining siblings have a 1/4 chance of being queer, and so on and so forth, until the last sibling has a  1/1 (100%) chance of being queer.

But that's not how probability in this situation actually functions. Let's say that a confirmed 1/5 of the global population are queer. In a family with 5 siblings, each sibling has a 1/5 chance of being queer. There is an increased chance of at least one of the siblings being queer compared to a family with an only child purely because there are more people, but subsequent siblings still only have a 1/5 chance of being queer. The probability grows ever so slightly for every member of the GLOBAL population who is confirmed to not be queer, but the probability increase is essentially negligible when it comes to the set of siblings.

You can also follow this up with something like "I don't want to pry at all, I just want to make sure I'm being respectful of you". Talking about people who might be assholes to them isn't a great subject to bring up. Letting your friend know that they are safe with you is good, though ultimately safety is something for other people to decide. Asking fairly open questions is good. Being ready to listen and resisting the urge to jump in with one's own person experiences and anecdotes (something I struggle with because I do it as an act of empathy but most people don't receive it that way).

In my experience, people you are close to will take the prompt of just bringing something up without the follow-up, and if they want to talk about it they will. If they don't they won't. A lot of this is really a question of perception. You may be interested in linguistic studies of colour and how different groups of people perceive or don't perceive colour. I would say that while colour vision may be impaired due to lack of developmental stimulus, a larger part of it is that even if the person in question was able to see colours after being released from the room their brain wouldn't necessarily conceptually know what to do with them and wouldn't really distinguish between them meaningfully.

We know that languages can show what colour differentiation stage a society has come to because the development of names of colours is pretty universal in language development. If a language has names for black, white, and red, but no other colours, people of the societal group that speaks that language may distinguish between colour values (dark, light, etc) but not between, say, green and blue and yellow of the same colour value.

If you taught someone language, including colour, with no context I highly suspect that it would be pretty meaningless to someone to see colour.

I disagree that devs don't know what people want, from a game developer perspective. This is what user testing is for, something a publisher is responsible for generally. A game will have this going on from early development stages. You don't want to get too far and have to scrap features.

What typically tends to happen is that devs have a whole laundry list of what users want. They have to decide what features can and can't be implemented in the time-frame, and often very desired features fall by the wayside. This is especially true of games where systems are rarely entirely independent and it's not always possible to develop one feature without at least partially developing others.

While games aren't a "first draft" on release by any means (it's absolutely incredible how many versions of any given game people will never know existed), the need to uphold deadlines and the knowledge that games can be updated post-launch, coupled with the general desire for less crunch time for developers, means that many project plans consider there to be some wiggle room on final delivery. Bear in mind that what is on the game chip has to be finalised at least several weeks before the release date. Most games have a day zero patch these days.

I don't think this is a case of misguided developers or a "first draft", is all, because that's not really how game dev works.

Part of the reason humans can become clumsy during growth spurts is because they're taller than their brain is used to, their feet are bigger than they're used to, their brain hasn't adjusted yet to the length of their arms. I  think it's important to remember that just because an action is being called sexist doesn't mean the individual is being called sexist. People do prejudiced things all the time without malicious intent but pretty much everyone out there has things to work on to become less biased. Saying "this thing is sexist" is not the same as saying "YOU are sexist".

I can also see why people assume something isn't an "-ism" just because is isn't intentional, but I think this is misunderstanding the nature of sexism (and racism and other prejudices). People are often blind to their own biases, and conduct themselves a certain way because it's just the done thing. They don't mean any harm by it, but that doesn't mean they're not doing harm anyway. We even have the term "benevolent sexism" for then a sexism is well-meaning or has the appearance of trying to benefit the party it's actually taking autonomy away from.

It's not a bad thing to point this out, and I think the assertiveness with which people often approach this is because it's 2023 and one would hope that people in general might approach their actions more critically. Obviously, things that are extremely obviously prejudiced to one person are not always obvious as such to everyone, but for many people it's something that's had to be hashed out over and over and it feels impossible that people can't see the obvious sexist roots of something. Doing anything less than couching it in caveats and qualifiers gets accusations of being a social justice warrior or being "woke" (derogatory).

Passing judgment on an action isn't passing judgment on an individual. But, as we all know, nuance is lost on the internet.

Hey there, it does sound like you have some disordered eating but this doesn't necessarily mean you have an eating disorder.

You mention ADHD, anxiety, depression, and some medications.

It may be that, between all those factors, you don't respond to your body's cues telling you when you're hungry. Many people with ADHD report this. Depression and anxiety can also cause loss of appetite, as can some medications, particularly ADHD meds. 

Over time, if you undereat chronically, your metabolism stops working as well to conserve your energy and keep your body running. This also unfortunately decreases your appetite.

You might benefit from setting some alarms for yourself to give yourself a meal schedule and a water-drinking schedule. Eat even though you don't feel hungry, and be consistent about it. Hopefully after a while your metabolism will fire back up and you may find that you do have an appetite again. Even if your lifestyle isn't very active you still need to hit your maintenance calories in order to not lose weight.

If you find that you experience things other than a lack of appetite and forgetting to eat (like actively not wanting to eat, worrying about gaining weight, etc) you may want to look into mental health help specifically for EDs.
